theme: O LORD, how many are my foes, David’s morning psalm
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 3. This is the first psalm in the Bible with a title that gives its setting: “A Psalm of David, when he fled from Absalom his son.” It is a morning prayer of trust in the face of danger.
settingTheScene: David wrote this psalm during the worst crisis of his reign, when his son Absalom led a rebellion and David had to flee Jerusalem. You will read that story in 2 Samuel 15 to 18. The psalm is placed here at the start of the stories about David. It shows what kind of man he was: when he was most afraid, he prayed. It is a prayer for a day that began in danger.
observation: “O LORD, how many are my foes! Many are rising against me” (v. 1).
“Many are saying of me, There is no salvation for him in God” (v. 2).
“But you, O LORD, are a shield about me, my glory, and the lifter of my head” (v. 3).
“I cried aloud to the LORD, and he answered me from his holy hill” (v. 4).
“I lay down and slept; I woke again, for the LORD sustained me” (v. 5).
“I will not be afraid of many thousands of people who have set themselves against me all around” (v. 6).
“Arise, O LORD! Save me, O my God!” (v. 7).
“Salvation belongs to the LORD; your blessing be on your people!” (v. 8).
interpretation:
The psalm begins with a list of problems. David has many enemies, and they are saying he is finished. It is the voice of discouragement: “There is no salvation for him in God.” The worst part of David’s trouble is not the armies but the taunt that God has abandoned him. This is the hardest thing for believers in distress: not simply the pain, but the suspicion that God is not there.

Then comes the great “But you.” David turns from the voices around him to the LORD. “But you, O LORD, are a shield about me.” A shield protects on every side. He is also “my glory,” meaning that even when David has lost his throne, his honor rests in God. And he is “the lifter of my head.” A defeated man hangs his head. God lifts it.

The most surprising line is verse 5: “I lay down and slept.” David is on the run from his own son, with an army in pursuit, and he sleeps. This is not carelessness. It is trust. He sleeps because “the LORD sustained me.” The sleep is a sign that he has given his anxiety to God. It is one of the most practical pictures of faith in the Bible.

He is not naive about the danger. He asks God to arise and save, and he describes God striking his enemies’ jaws. The psalm ends with a statement that is a creed in four words: “Salvation belongs to the LORD.” David cannot save himself, and neither can anyone else.

Even in a bitter family conflict, with his own son against him, David prays, “Your blessing be on your people.” He does not forget the nation. In his distress, he thinks of others.
connection: Jesus slept in a boat during a storm (Mark 4:38), showing the same trust. He too was betrayed by someone close, and he crossed the Kidron valley into a garden (John 18:1). Paul says, “We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed” (2 Corinthians 4:8). Hebrews 12:2 says that Jesus “for the joy that was set before him endured the cross.” Revelation 7:10 declares, “Salvation belongs to our God.”
application:
Pray this psalm tonight before you go to sleep, and entrust your worries to God.

Think about the voices that say there is no help for you in God. Answer them with “But you, O LORD.”

Pray a blessing over your church and your nation.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he is a shield about you, and tell him about those who rise against you.
Ask him to let you sleep in his care.
Bless his people in your own words.
